clue.text: Tiddly oaf never shakes? I don't believe it

indicators.note: tiddly is British slang for slightly drunk, and drunken words stagger out of order

parts.note: all fourteen letters of these three words are the raw material

explanation.surface: A tipsy lout who never trembles provokes an exasperated cry of disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiddly means mildly drunk in British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an exclamation of exasperated disbelief, used just as one might say 'I don't believe it!'

clue.text: Early bit of devotion: rousing her at four

indicators.note: rousing stirs things up, so the following letters are shaken into a fresh order

parts.note: the nine letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is woken at four in the morning for early prayers.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer opens the Lord's Prayer, so it is literally the early bit of a devotion; 'Early' also suits the four a.m. scene.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the opening words of the Lord's Prayer, the first portion of a familiar Christian devotion.

clue.text: Cobbler does this for despicable people

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a shoemaker fits new ... to shoes, a verb
second meaning: cads or rotters, a plural noun

explanation.surface: A shoe-mender works for nasty customers.
explanation.definitionFit: To heel a shoe is to repair its heel, a cobbler's task; heels is also slang for contemptible, untrustworthy men.

clue.text: Amoral foe tampered with sports car

indicators.note: something tampered with has been interfered with and messed about, so its letters are disturbed

parts.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An unprincipled enemy has sabotaged someone's sports car.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian marque, based in Milan, builds high-performance sporty motor vehicles.

clue.text: Wild deer on both sides of river went astray

indicators.note: the scrambled letters sit on either side, so they wrap around what follows
wild things run free and unruly, so the animal's letters are scattered

parts.note: taken as written, then scrambled
R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Wild deer graze along both banks of a river and wander off course.
explanation.definitionFit: To err is to make a mistake or stray from the right path, so its past tense matches wandered off course.

clue.text: Big mugs muffled passage on fancy keyboard instruments

indicators.note: to muffle is to wrap something up, so the first item encloses the second

parts.note: steins are large beer mugs
a way is a route or passage

explanation.surface: Beer drinkers' tankards deaden the sound of a passage played on posh pianos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passage' suggests a piece of music in the piano scene, but it means a route.
explanation.definitionFit: Steinway is a prestigious maker of concert grand pianos, so its instruments are luxurious keyboard instruments.

clue.text: Fatalist will lose weight to become famous

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away, so letters drop out of the first word

parts.note: taken as written
fat is body weight, as in putting on fat

explanation.surface: A gloomy fatalist goes on a diet hoping to become a celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: The A-list is the top tier of celebrities, so as an adjective it describes someone very well known.

clue.text: Oriental festival supported by nationalist

indicators.note: in a down clue, being supported means sitting on top, so the next piece goes underneath

parts.note: Easter is the Christian spring festival
N is an abbreviation for nationalist

explanation.surface: A spring celebration is backed by a nationalist politician.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe things belonging to or coming from Asia and the East.

clue.text: Quarrelling dads to wrestle

indicators.note: wrestling twists and tangles bodies, so the letters are twisted into a new arrangement

parts.note: the six letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Fathers squabble and come to blows.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in disagreement or conflict with someone is the idiomatic sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Brief gives bum steer

indicators.note: bum is slang for bad or faulty, so the next word is wrongly arranged

parts.note: the five letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone's short reply sends you in the wrong direction.
explanation.walkthrough: A bum steer is a piece of misleading advice; 'bum' as faulty does the work.
explanation.definitionFit: Brief and curt both describe speech or writing that uses few words, sometimes abruptly.

clue.text: Spice Girl given cautions about counterfeit goods

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the warnings go round the pop star

parts.note: a golfer shouts fore as a warning
Geri Halliwell was Ginger Spice in the Spice Girls

explanation.surface: A pop star is warned about selling knock-off merchandise.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spice Girls were a 1990s British girl band; Geri is the member usually used in clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Fakes made to pass as genuine articles are exactly what fraudulent counterfeit products are.

clue.text: Traditional intro in Raiders remake

indicators.note: a remake reshapes an old film, so the word is rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: the seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A classic opening sequence appears in a new version of the Raiders film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intro' suggests a film's title sequence; it is the opening of a formal letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the customary formal salutation that begins a business letter to an unnamed man.

clue.text: Web implicated, diet abandoned where people eat

indicators.note: something implicated is involved or caught up inside, so the first word goes within
abandoned means wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose

parts.note: taken as written, then scrambled
a net is a web of mesh

explanation.surface: Internet involvement leads someone to give up their diet and head for a restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: A dinette is a small dining area or alcove off a kitchen, a place for meals.

clue.text: 'Uh' sound elicited by kitsch wardrobe

indicators.note: to elicit is to draw something out, so the letters are drawn out of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone groans 'uh' at the sight of a tacky wardrobe.
explanation.definitionFit: In phonetics this is the neutral unstressed vowel, written as an upside-down e, heard in words like about.

clue.text: Religious leader with a 'tally-ho!': a maverick

indicators.note: a maverick refuses to follow the herd, so the letters break from their order

parts.note: all nine letters, both single-letter words included

explanation.surface: An unconventional cleric joins a fox hunt shouting the huntsman's cry.
explanation.walkthrough: Tally-ho is the cry of the British fox hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: An ayatollah is a senior Shia Muslim cleric, especially in Iran, so a high clergyman.

clue.text: Arbitration with no time for deep thought

indicators.note: having none of something means it is removed from the longer word

parts.note: meditation is deep contemplation
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Busy negotiators settling a dispute have no time to sit and reflect.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are processes in which a neutral third party helps settle a dispute between two sides.

clue.text: Seat of learning choosy lad declined

indicators.note: declined suggests bent or turned down, so the letters are turned into another order

parts.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A fussy boy turned down a place at college.
explanation.definitionFit: A school whose pupils go home each evening, rather than boarding, is an institution of education.

clue.text: 19, simple-minded one

parts.note: innocent can mean naive or guileless
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.walkthrough: The 19 refers to the answer at 19 down, a pope; this one is the fifth-century bishop of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Innocent I was an early Pope, so he fits the papal leader described by 19 down's answer.

clue.text: Suffering when a conservative follows heartless, reactionary group

indicators.note: follows says the political pieces come after the reversed word
reactionary suggests going backwards, so the word is read in reverse
without a heart means the central letter of the word is cut out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Political misery when a Tory joins a cruel right-wing faction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reactionary' looks political, matching the Tory, but it signals going back.
explanation.definitionFit: Purgatory is a place or state of torment and misery, used loosely for any ordeal.

clue.text: Religious leader quiet concerning difference of opinion

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for soft
on means about or regarding
a tiff is a minor quarrel

explanation.surface: A churchman quietly addresses a dispute.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pope is called the Supreme Pontiff, head of the Roman Catholic Church.

clue.text: Act immorally with American in snotty enclosure

indicators.note: with says the second piece is placed alongside the first

parts.note: to sin is to do wrong
US is the abbreviation for American, as in US citizen

explanation.surface: Someone misbehaves with an American inside a snooty private enclave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snotty' reads as snooty, but here it means full of mucus.
explanation.definitionFit: A sinus is a hollow cavity in the skull bones around the nose, where mucus collects with a cold.

clue.text: Primarily, somewhere you don't necessarily expect Yukonese?

definitions.text: somewhere you don't necessarily expect Yukonese

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of each word counts

parts.words: somewhere you don't necessarily expect Yukonese
parts.note: the initial letters of these six words

explanation.surface: A wry remark that people from the Yukon are not what you would expect to find in a certain place.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: an Australian city is a place you would not expect Canadians from the Yukon.
explanation.definitionFit: Sydney, in Australia, is far from the Canadian Yukon, so it is an unlikely spot to meet people from there.

clue.text: On 'scone', rendering given by reactionaries

indicators.note: a rendering is a new version or interpretation, so the letters are presented differently

parts.note: the seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Diehard conservatives deliver their pronunciation of scone, rhyming with gone or with cone.
explanation.walkthrough: How to say scone is a famous British argument, which fits the reactionaries.
explanation.definitionFit: Neocons are neoconservatives, right-wing hawks often called reactionary by their critics.

clue.text: As an alternative, including the alternative

indicators.note: including means holding within, so the first piece goes around the second

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pedantic note on wording: offering one option while also mentioning another.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word is the setter's trick: the first phrase gives a two-letter conjunction, while the last word alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The other one is the remaining choice, a second option, so an alternative.

clue.text: Small potatoes!? A tremendous success!

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
mash is mashed potatoes

explanation.surface: A stage show is dismissed as unimportant, then turns out to be a huge hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small potatoes' is an idiom for something trivial, which hides the split into two separate words.
explanation.definitionFit: A smash, or smash hit, is a show, record or film that wins enormous popular acclaim.

clue.text: Batman's seen in this hoax in American resort

parts.note: the superhero always wears a cape
cod is British slang for a hoax or fake, as in cod science

explanation.surface: A Batman sighting turns out to be a hoax at a holiday spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Cape Cod is a hooked peninsula in Massachusetts famous for beaches and summer holiday towns.

clue.text: Scotsman in post office, one of 6

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the man goes within the office

parts.note: PO is the abbreviation for post office
Ian is a typically Scottish first name

explanation.surface: A Scot is standing in the post office queue.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 refers to 6 down, a famous make of piano, so one of them is a single instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Steinways are pianos, so a single example of the 6 down answer is one such keyboard instrument.

clue.text: Bisected protozoan — 50% missing very soon

indicators.note: with half absent, only the first part of the creature's name survives

parts.note: bisected means cut into two
an amoeba is a single-celled organism

explanation.surface: A single-celled creature is split down the middle and half of it vanishes.
explanation.walkthrough: A mo is British informal for a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal British idiom promising something will happen shortly, in a brief moment.

clue.text: Nannies essentially depicted in musical movie

indicators.note: essentially points to the essence or core, so the outer letters are dropped

parts.note: the inner letters, losing the first and last

explanation.surface: Childminders are shown in a film with songs.
explanation.walkthrough: Fitting, since the story's orphan heroine is cared for, though not by nannies.
explanation.definitionFit: Annie is a stage musical about a red-haired orphan, adapted as a song-filled film more than once.

clue.text: Bashed fifth toe? Holler just because you can

indicators.note: something bashed is knocked out of shape, so these letters are battered into a new order

parts.note: all fourteen letters to rearrange, ignoring the question mark

explanation.surface: Someone stubs their little toe and yells.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes doing something for no reason other than amusement, purely on a whim.
